Blocks 39 and 68 checked the attention weights only at the whole-matrix level: whether heads were swapped across layers, and whether RoPE frequency-band capacity looked normal. No component of the attention mechanism has been tested causally. Nobody has asked what answer tokens read from the end of the prompt, where the 66 "solve-math" neurons fire.

The global-layer attention patterns from pass 7 (text A, one of the model's own correct answers) let me check this cheaply. For each global head, I will measure how much answer tokens attend to the BOS sink, the problem body, the instruction, the final template tokens ("<end_of_turn>\n<start_of_turn>model\n") and the answer itself.

If some head reads the last prompt tokens heavily, the mode decided there (LaTeX vs markdown, and possibly a brake) is broadcast to every answer token through that head. That would make "ablate the source neurons" or "ablate that head" a well-founded causal test. If no head reads them, a mode stored at the last prompt token can reach the answer only weakly, and I will rank the U1 test (ablating the 66 neurons) lower.

First I need the file layout of fwd_7.

Text A has 244 tokens, with full attention maps for the four global layers. I will split the positions into BOS, opening template, problem body, instruction, closing template (the last 5 prompt tokens, from "<end_of_turn>" through "model\n"), and answer.

For every global head, I will then measure the mean attention mass from answer tokens onto each region, plus the mass on the single last prompt token. A head that puts, say, more than 20% of its attention on the closing template would be the channel that carries the prompt-time "mode" into every answer token. That would justify a causal test of the 66 last-token "solve-math" neurons or of that head. If every head reads mainly BOS, the problem and nearby answer tokens, the mode channel goes through local layers or is weak.

Attention from answer tokens to the end of the prompt is concentrated in the global layer 11. Heads L11h2 and L11h3 put about 26% of their attention on the single last prompt token, the "\n" after "model", and L11h0 puts 9% there. They use that token almost like a sink: L11h2 puts only 4% on BOS, where the other global heads put 20–48%.

So L11 broadcasts the state at the last prompt token to every answer token, and the 66 "solve-math" neurons fire exactly at that token. They respond only to a math problem combined with the solve instruction. This gives a concrete candidate circuit: task-specific neurons write a "mode" at the end of the prompt, and L11h2/h3 copy it into the whole answer.

D1 already removed one direction of that mode (dm[10]) and changed only the style. But the 66 neurons were never ablated causally, and their writes may carry more than dm[10]. Before spending a pass, I will recover exactly how I selected them, from blocks 54 and 55, so the ablation uses that list and not a new selection.

Block 55 defined the 66 neurons by strict criteria: effect size of at least 6 against all three control groups (math+translate, nonmath, nonmath+instruction), the same sign, and |activation| ≥ 0.5 at the last prompt token. They are stored in the kernel variable `S` as layer → neuron list.

Before ablating them, I want to know whether their combined write at the last prompt token is something D1 already removed. I will fold each layer's combined write, the G1-mean activation times the down-proj columns, through that layer's post-feedforward norm scale. Then I compare it with the D1 direction and measure its size.

If the writes are mostly parallel to D1, ablating these neurons would largely repeat D1's style-only effect, and I would rank the test low. If they are largely orthogonal to D1 and substantial, the U1 ablation tests a new channel: the "math-task" state at the end of the prompt that L11h2/h3 broadcast. Then it is worth a pass.
